evidence.title: When a Sensor Loses Its Oracle: Three-Arm Differential Observability and Zero-Oracle Fail-Closed Abstention for Membrane Fouling Diagnostics
evidence.abstract:
Soft sensors for reverse osmosis (RO) and forward osmosis (FO) desalination must separate reversible concentration polarization (CP) from irreversible mineral scaling and biofouling while remaining resilient to sensor drift, temperature shocks, and reference-channel contamination. We identify two structural vulnerabilities in differential membrane diagnostics: (1) a 2-arm differential cartridge cannot distinguish reference-arm contamination from test-arm cleanliness, producing a 71.17% estimation error without warning under 10% partial reference fouling (Scenario NC5), whereas a 3-arm differential manifold with a witness-ratio guard (τref = |rref(t) − rref,0|/rref,0 > 0.03) restores Rank-2 Fisher observability (det I > 0) and cuts error to 7.72%; and (2) autonomous diagnostic codebases suffer from oracle leakage when simulator ground-truth fields (ground_truth_scale_um) or synthetic nominal reference values remain accessible inside production classes or when invariants rely on strip-prone assert statements under python -O. evidence.title: Water Treatment for "Green" Hydrogen Production in Alkaline Electrolyzers
evidence.abstract: This paper systematizes typical feedwater quality requirements for AWE systems and explains why the parameters of specific electrical resistance (resistivity) and electrical conductivity are interrelated quality-control indicators. The main technological solutions for producing demineralized water are reviewed, including mechanical filtration, activated carbon filtration, reverse osmosis (RO), and electrodeionization (EDI). Key operational risks are also discussed, such as channeling, increased pressure drop (ΔP), carryover of carbon fines, biofouling, and oxidative damage to RO membranes. As a practical example, an aggregated process scheme is presented for a water treatment line designed to produce demineralized (DM) water with a target quality of approximately 1 MΩ·cm or higher. Recommendations are provided for monitoring (conductivity/resistivity, SiO₂, TOC, Cl⁻, iron), filter backwash regimes, protection of RO membranes from chlorine, and reduction of factors that contribute to increased cell voltage during AWE operation.

evidence.title: Plasma-Enhanced Magnetron Sputtering: A Novel Approach for Biofunctional Metal Nanoparticle Coatings on Reverse Osmosis Composite Membranes
evidence.abstract: Reverse osmosis (RO) is the most common method for treating salt and brackish water. As a membrane-driven process, a key challenge for RO systems is their susceptibility to scaling and biofouling. To address these issues, functional coatings utilizing metal nanoparticles (MNPs) are developed. In this study, silver, gold, and copper nanoparticles are applied onto thin-film composite (TFC) membranes using plasma-enhanced magnetron sputtering. The elemental composition, surface morphology, and hydrophilicity of the coatings are analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and contact angle measurements. The antimicrobial properties and the filtration efficiency of the coated membranes are assessed through application-specific experimental setups. Silver and copper nanoparticles exhibit superior antimicrobial properties, reducing microorganism adhesion by a factor of 103 compared to uncoated membranes. Under appropriate coating conditions, no deterioration in filtration performance is observed. Enhancing the adhesion of MNPs is necessary for achieving sustained release of metal ions.

evidence.title: Ideal Desalination through Graphyne-4 Membrane: Nanopores for Quantized Water Transport
evidence.abstract: Graphyne-4 sheet exhibits promising potential for nanoscale desalination to achieve both high water permeability and salt rejection rate. Extensive molecular dynamics simulations on pore-size effects suggest that graphyne-4, with 4 acetylene bonds between two adjacent phenyl rings, has the best performance with 100% salt rejection and an unprecedented water permeability, to our knowledge, of ~13L/cm2/day/MPa, about 10 times higher than the state-of-the-art nanoporous graphene reported previously (Nano Lett.s 2012, 12, 3602-3608). In addition, the membrane entails very low energy consumption for producing 1m3 of fresh water, i.e., 3.6e-3 kWh/m3, three orders of magnitude less than the prevailing commercial membranes based on reverse osmosis. Water flow rate across the graphyne-4 sheet exhibits intriguing nonlinear dependence on the pore size owing to the quantized nature of water flow at the nanoscale. Such novel transport behavior has important implications to the design of highly effective and efficient desalination membranes.

evidence.title: High-flux water desalination with interfacial salt sieving effect in nanoporous carbon composite membranes
evidence.abstract: Nanoporous carbon composite membranes, comprising a layer of porous carbon fiber structures with an average channel width of 30-60 nm grown on a porous ceramic substrate, are found to exhibit robust desalination effect with high freshwater flux. In three different membrane processes of vacuum membrane distillation, reverse osmosis and forward osmosis, the carbon composite membrane showed 100% salt rejection with 3.5 to 20 times higher freshwater flux compared to existing polymeric membranes. Thermal accounting experiments found that at least 80% of the freshwater pass through the carbon composite membrane with no phase change. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a unique salt rejection mechanism. When seawater is interfaced with either vapor or the surface of carbon, one to three interfacial atomic layers contain no salt ions. Below the liquid entry pressure, the salt solution is stopped at the openings to the porous channels and forms a meniscus, while the surface layer of freshwater can feed the surface diffusion flux that is fast-transported on the surfaces of the carbon fibers, driven by the chemical potential gradient. As the surface-transported water does not involve a phase change, hence that component involves no energy expenditure in the form of latent heat.

evidence.title: Mathematical modelling and numerical simulation of reverse-osmosis desalination
evidence.abstract: The reverse osmosis membrane module is an integral element of a desalination system as it determines the overall performance of the desalination plant. The fraction of clean water that can be recovered via this process is often limited by salt precipitation which plays a critical role in its sustainability. In this work, we present a model to study the complex interplay between flow, transport and precipitation processes in reverse osmosis membranes, which together influence recovery and in turn process sustainability. A reactive porous interface model describes the membrane with a dynamic evolving porosity and permeability to capture the scaling and clogging of the membrane. An open-source finite-volume numerical solver is implemented within the OpenFOAM library and numerical tests are presented here showing the effect of the various parameters of the model and the robustness of the model to describe a wide range of operating conditions.

evidence.title: Quantifying the Trade-offs between Energy Consumption and Salt Removal Rate in Membrane-free Cation Intercalation Desalination
evidence.abstract: Electrochemical desalination devices that use redox-active cation intercalation electrodes show promise for desalination of salt-rich water resources with high water recovery and low energy consumption. While previous modeling and experiments used ion-exchange membranes to maximize charge efficiency, here a membrane-free alternative is evaluated to reduce capital cost by using a porous diaphragm to separate Na$_{1+x}$NiFe(CN)$_6$ electrodes. Two-dimensional porous-electrode modeling shows that, while charge efficiency losses are inherent to a diaphragm-based architecture, charge efficiency values approaching the anion transference number (61$\%$ for NaCl) are achievable for diaphragms with sufficiently low salt conductance. Closed-form equations are thereby derived that relate charge efficiency to the non-dimensional Pèclet and Damköhler numbers that enable the selection of current and flow velocity to produce a desired degree of desalination. Simulations using these conditions are used to quantify the tradeoffs between energy consumption and salt removal rate for diaphragm-based cells operated at a range of currents. The simulated distributions of reactions are shown to result from the local salt concentration variations within electrodes using diffusion-potential theory. We also simulate the cycling dynamics of various flow configurations and show that flow-through electrodes exceed the degree-of-desalination compared with flow-by and flow-behind configurations due to solution stagnation within electrodes.

evidence.title: Three waves of chemical dynamics
evidence.abstract: Three epochs in development of chemical dynamics are presented. We try to understand the modern research programs in the light of classical works. Three eras (or waves) of chemical dynamics can be revealed in the flux of research and publications. These waves may be associated with leaders: the first is the van't Hoof wave, the second may be called the Semenov--Hinshelwood wave and the third is definitely the Aris wave. Of course, the whole building was impossible without efforts of hundreds of other researchers. Some of of them are mentioned in our brief review.

evidence.title: The Effect of Frequency Droop Damping on System Parameters and Battery Sizing During Load Change Condition
evidence.abstract: Inverter-based resources (IBR) have been widely studied for their advantages on the current power systems. This increase in the penetration of renewable energy has raised some concerns about the stability of the existing grid. Historically, power systems are dominated by synchronous generators that can easily react to system instability due to high inertia and damping characteristics. However, with IBR, the control of the inverter plays a crucial role in contributing to the system stability and enhancing the functionality of the inverters. One of these novel control methods is droop control. Droop characteristics are used to control voltage, frequency, and active and reactive power. This paper presents the impact of frequency droop damping on system frequency, real power, and the rate of change of frequency with distributed energy resources. Also, battery sizing is suggested based on the results. The results also show the need for optimal selection for the frequency droop damping to fulfill the appropriate battery size in terms of cost and performance. The simulations are carried out in an electromagnetic transient program (EMTP)

Key operational risks are also discussed, such as channeling, increased pressure drop (ΔP), carryover of carbon fines, biofouling, and oxidative damage to RO membranes. As a practical example, an aggregated process scheme is presented for a water treatment line designed to produce demineralized (DM) water with a target quality of approximately 1 MΩ·cm or higher. Recommendations are provided for monitoring (conductivity/resistivity, SiO₂, TOC, Cl⁻, iron), filter backwash regimes, protection of RO membranes from chlorine, and reduction of factors that contribute to increased cell voltage during AWE operation.

system.value: Plasma-Enhanced Magnetron Sputtering: A Novel Approach for Biofunctional Metal Nanoparticle Coatings on Reverse Osmosis Composite Membranes

abstract.value: Reverse osmosis (RO) is the most common method for treating salt and brackish water. As a membrane-driven process, a key challenge for RO systems is their susceptibility to scaling and biofouling. To address these issues, functional coatings utilizing metal nanoparticles (MNPs) are developed. In this study, silver, gold, and copper nanoparticles are applied onto thin-film composite (TFC) membranes using plasma-enhanced magnetron sputtering. The elemental composition, surface morphology, and hydrophilicity of the coatings are analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and contact angle measurements. The antimicrobial properties and the filtration efficiency of the coated membranes are assessed through application-specific experimental setups. Silver and copper nanoparticles exhibit superior antimicrobial properties, reducing microorganism adhesion by a factor of 103 compared to uncoated membranes. Under appropriate coating conditions, no deterioration in filtration performance is observed. Enhancing the adhesion of MNPs is necessary for achieving sustained release of metal ions.

system.value: Ideal Desalination through Graphyne-4 Membrane: Nanopores for Quantized Water Transport

abstract.value: Graphyne-4 sheet exhibits promising potential for nanoscale desalination to achieve both high water permeability and salt rejection rate. Extensive molecular dynamics simulations on pore-size effects suggest that graphyne-4, with 4 acetylene bonds between two adjacent phenyl rings, has the best performance with 100% salt rejection and an unprecedented water permeability, to our knowledge, of ~13L/cm2/day/MPa, about 10 times higher than the state-of-the-art nanoporous graphene reported previously (Nano Lett.s 2012, 12, 3602-3608). In addition, the membrane entails very low energy consumption for producing 1m3 of fresh water, i.e., 3.6e-3 kWh/m3, three orders of magnitude less than the prevailing commercial membranes based on reverse osmosis. Water flow rate across the graphyne-4 sheet exhibits intriguing nonlinear dependence on the pore size owing to the quantized nature of water flow at the nanoscale. Such novel transport behavior has important implications to the design of highly effective and efficient desalination membranes.

system.value: High-flux water desalination with interfacial salt sieving effect in nanoporous carbon composite membranes

abstract.value: Nanoporous carbon composite membranes, comprising a layer of porous carbon fiber structures with an average channel width of 30-60 nm grown on a porous ceramic substrate, are found to exhibit robust desalination effect with high freshwater flux. In three different membrane processes of vacuum membrane distillation, reverse osmosis and forward osmosis, the carbon composite membrane showed 100% salt rejection with 3.5 to 20 times higher freshwater flux compared to existing polymeric membranes. Thermal accounting experiments found that at least 80% of the freshwater pass through the carbon composite membrane with no phase change. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a unique salt rejection mechanism. When seawater is interfaced with either vapor or the surface of carbon, one to three interfacial atomic layers contain no salt ions. Below the liquid entry pressure, the salt solution is stopped at the openings to the porous channels and forms a meniscus, while the surface layer of freshwater can feed the surface diffusion flux that is fast-transported on the surfaces of the carbon fibers, driven by the chemical potential gradient. As the surface-transported water does not involve a phase change, hence that component involves no energy expenditure in the form of latent heat.

system.value: Mathematical modelling and numerical simulation of reverse-osmosis desalination

abstract.value: The reverse osmosis membrane module is an integral element of a desalination system as it determines the overall performance of the desalination plant. The fraction of clean water that can be recovered via this process is often limited by salt precipitation which plays a critical role in its sustainability. In this work, we present a model to study the complex interplay between flow, transport and precipitation processes in reverse osmosis membranes, which together influence recovery and in turn process sustainability. A reactive porous interface model describes the membrane with a dynamic evolving porosity and permeability to capture the scaling and clogging of the membrane. An open-source finite-volume numerical solver is implemented within the OpenFOAM library and numerical tests are presented here showing the effect of the various parameters of the model and the robustness of the model to describe a wide range of operating conditions.

cemetery_warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

cemetery_warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

cemetery_warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.
cemetery_warnings.action_required: Explicit justification required to proceed despite this constraint

The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.

cemetery_warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

candidates.intervention: Retrofit the 40,000 m3/day RO train's monitoring system with a three-arm differential cartridge: Arm 1 (Test) measures pressure drop across the specific membrane stack experiencing flux droop; Arm 2 (Reference) measures pressure drop across a parallel clean-water loop or a dedicated witness stack with identical flow conditions but isolated feed; Arm 3 (Feed) measures upstream pressure to isolate system hydraulic effects. Implement a witness-ratio guard that triggers a fail-closed abstention when |rref(t) - rref,0|/rref,0 exceeds 0.03, preventing CIP initiation based on contaminated reference data.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: Three-arm differential observability via witness-ratio guard, where a physical reference arm monitors membrane resistance independently of the test arm; this separates reversible concentration polarization (CP) from irreversible biofouling by detecting reference-channel contamination through a normalized drift threshold (τref), restoring Fisher observability and preventing false-negative fouling diagnoses.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Retrofit the 40,000 m3/day RO train's monitoring system with a three-arm differential cartridge: Arm 1 (Test) measures pressure drop across the specific membrane stack experiencing flux droop; Arm 2 (Reference) measures pressure drop across a parallel clean-water loop or a dedicated witness stack with identical flow conditions but isolated feed; Arm 3 (Feed) measures upstream pressure to isolate system hydraulic effects. Implement a witness-ratio guard that triggers a fail-closed abstention when |rref(t) - rref,0|/rref,0 exceeds 0.03, preventing CIP initiation based on contaminated reference data.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: Zero-oracle fail-closed abstention, where the diagnostic codebase is hardened to remove all access to simulator ground-truth fields or synthetic nominal references, forcing the system to reject a diagnosis if a physical reference channel is missing or inconsistent; this eliminates "false-confident commits" where the system incorrectly certifies a healthy membrane state due to leakage of idealized parameters into production logic.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Refactor the plant's autonomous diagnostic software for the 40,000 m3/day RO train to enforce explicit runtime ValueError guards instead of strip-prone assert statements; strip all simulator ground-truth fields (e.g., ground_truth_scale_um) and synthetic nominal reference values from the production class; implement a "ABSTAIN_MISSING_REFERENCE_EVIDENCE" flag that prevents CIP scheduling unless a valid physical reference evidence chain is established.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: Differential separation of reversible Concentration Polarization (CP) from irreversible biofouling using a soft-sensor that isolates the reversible component (driving force loss) from the irreversible component (membrane resistance increase), allowing the system to distinguish temporary flux droop from permanent membrane degradation without chemical cleaning.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Implement a soft-sensor algorithm in the RO control system that continuously calculates the reversible CP loss by extrapolating flux at zero concentration difference, and compares it to the measured flux; the system triggers a CIP only when the irreversible residual (total resistance - CP resistance) exceeds a threshold, rather than when total flux drops; this leverages the "separation of reversible CP from irreversible... biofouling" capability.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The same Rank-2 Fisher observability mechanism via a third reference channel, applied to the target system's membrane modules: by installing a dedicated "witness" pressure/flux channel that monitors a clean reference section, the causal chain transfers to decouple the reversible concentration polarization signal from irreversible biofouling resistance, preventing the diagnostic "false confidence" that triggers premature or mis-timed CIP.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Retrofit the 40,000 m3/d SWRO train with a three-arm differential manifold for each pressure vessel section, where the third arm acts as a clean reference witness, replacing the current two-arm flux/pressure differential monitoring.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The same fail-closed zero-oracle abstention mechanism, applied to the plant's autonomous control logic: by stripping simulator ground-truth fields and enforcing explicit runtime guards, the causal chain transfers to a "fail-closed" state where the controller refuses to commit to a clean/dirty classification (and thus refuses to trigger CIP) when reference evidence is insufficient, replacing the current "false-confident" auto-CIP trigger with an explicit abort state.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Harden the plant's autonomous diagnostic codebase (CommercialPhysicalWitnessB equivalent) to remove all synthetic nominal reference values and replace strip-prone assert statements with explicit ValueError runtime guards, enforcing a 100% clean operating-sweep coverage before allowing autonomous decisions.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The same differential observability mechanism via two-arm vs. three-arm structural comparison, applied to the constraint of no chlorine-based disinfection: the causal chain transfers to the recognition that the current two-arm differential cartridge (flux vs. pressure) cannot distinguish reference-arm contamination (e.g., biofilm on a reference sensor) from test-arm cleanliness, leading to misdiagnosis of biofouling as concentration polarization, which triggers ineffective CIP cycles because the root cause (biofilm) is not chemically targeted by standard CIP if misidentified, or forces the plant to violate recovery constraints by reducing flux.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Deploy a three-arm differential manifold that explicitly isolates the biofilm fouling signal from the reversible concentration polarization signal, allowing the plant to maintain permeate recovery by managing the CP component (via flow rate adjustments) while targeting only the irreversible biofilm component with CIP, avoiding the 71.17% estimation error that leads to over-frequent cleaning.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The causal mechanism is the restoration of Rank-2 Fisher observability in a differential sensing topology, which allows the system to distinguish between reversible concentration polarization and irreversible fouling by utilizing a third independent channel (witness arm) that provides a guard against reference-channel contamination. This is domain knowledge of differential observability theory combined with the record's evidence that a 3-arm manifold resolves the ambiguity present in 2-arm systems.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Replace the standard two-channel differential pressure/flux monitoring on individual RO modules with a three-arm differential manifold configuration where one arm serves as a dedicated 'witness' channel subject to a ratio guard (τref) to validate the integrity of the reference signal before committing to a fouling diagnosis.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The causal mechanism is "fail-closed abstention," where the diagnostic algorithm is designed to explicitly withhold a fouling verdict (abstain) rather than commit a false-confident diagnosis when physical reference evidence is missing or invalid. This is a control-systems design principle (fault detection and isolation via logical guards) supported by the record's evidence that hardening the code to remove oracle leakage and enforce runtime guards reduces false-confident commits.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Implement a zero-oracle diagnostic software layer on the plant's SCADA/DCS system that replaces ground-truth-dependent asserts with explicit runtime ValueError guards. The system is configured to output an "ABSTAIN_MISSING_REFERENCE_EVIDENCE" flag whenever the witness-ratio guard (from Hypothesis 1) indicates reference contamination or when a reference channel is unavailable, preventing automated CIP triggers based on corrupted data.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The causal mechanism is the isolation of the "physical witness" from simulator ground-truth fields to ensure that the diagnostic inference is based solely on measured physical quantities (pressure, flux) rather than synthetic reference values. This is a software engineering integrity principle (decoupling simulation artifacts from production logic) combined with the record's evidence that removing `ground_truth_scale_um` and synthetic nominal values hardens the system against oracle leakage.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Refactor the diagnostic codebase to completely remove access to simulator ground-truth fields and synthetic nominal references from the production class `CommercialPhysicalWitnessB`. The system is restructured so that all invariant checks are performed against physical sensor readings and the witness-ratio derived from the 3-arm manifold (Hypothesis 1), ensuring that the "zero-oracle" estimator relies exclusively on measurable physical state.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: Domain knowledge of low-shear flow dynamics indicates that increasing linear velocity at membrane surfaces reduces the concentration boundary layer thickness ($\delta_c$) and shear stress, thereby inhibiting the initial attachment and maturation of biofilms; the record’s evidence is the 15% normalized flux droop, which signals significant mass transfer limitation and fouling accumulation on the membrane surface.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Retrofit the RO high-pressure pump system or adjust valve settings to increase crossflow velocity by 10–15% to enhance hydrodynamic shear on the membrane surface.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: Domain knowledge of biofouling kinetics shows that intermittent backwashing disrupts the extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) of early-stage biofilms before they mature into mature, resistant structures; the record’s evidence is the constraint against chlorine-based disinfection, which necessitates a non-oxidizing, physical/mechanical mitigation strategy for the biofilm fouling.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Implement periodic permeate backwashing by reversing the flow through the membrane elements for 10–15 minutes every 4 hours.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: Domain knowledge of microbial physiology indicates that biofilm growth is highly temperature-dependent and that nutrient availability (dissolved organic carbon) supports microbial metabolism; the record’s evidence is the specific device context (SWRO at 40,000 m3/day) where feedwater quality and temperature are controlled variables that can be manipulated to reduce microbial carrying capacity without violating the chlorine constraint.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Pre-treatment thermal conditioning or precise temperature control of feedwater to maintain lower inlet temperatures, or advanced biological pre-treatment (e.g., UV-A pretreatment without oxidation) to reduce the organic carbon fraction available for biofilm formation.

CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.justification: R377 patent-text ground truth (TOSCANINI/R377_PATENT_TEXT_FETCH.json + R377_PATENT_TEXT_GROUND_TRUTH.json): 12/30 family representatives (40%) were substantively irrelevant cross-domain term collisions (CWDM optical link for a battery-thermal candidate; dental-condition monitoring for rolling stock; bone fracture forceps for rail steel...). A hit sharing NO entity term with the candidate now needs >= 3 NON-generic mechanism terms to be mechanism art: the measured true cross-domain analog (line-pipe steel with hydrogen fracture toughness for a rail-steel candidate) shares 3 non-generic terms and survives; every measured false positive shares <= 2 and is demoted. This RAISES the cross-domain bar (was the same >= 2 as same-domain) — stricter, not weaker (Art. VII).
CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.uncertainty: term overlap remains a proxy; entity word-sense collisions ('gear': steering vs draft) can still pass — disclosed limitation, not a solved problem

MIN_MECHANISM_OVERLAP.justification: same term-overlap rule family as the pipeline relevance adjudicator and the Q2 instrument (>= 2 shared content terms = domain-specific rather than accidental collision); NOT weakened relative to any prior gate
MIN_MECHANISM_OVERLAP.uncertainty: term overlap is a proxy for mechanism identity

ANTICIPATION_COVERAGE_RATIO.justification: a family ANTICIPATES only when nearly ALL elements of the candidate's FULL distinguishing set (uncapped — the claim elements, not the 6-term query core) appear in the family's claim/abstract text; 0.8 leaves a >= 20% element margin — anything lower would convert partial art into a kill (Art. XXVIII forbids). Measured adversarial case: a domain-only patent reached 0.857 against a capped denominator whose true differentiators (acoustic, multi-modal) had been ranked out
ANTICIPATION_COVERAGE_RATIO.uncertainty: claim coverage measured by term overlap, not a claim chart; recorded per family with evidence tier

Soft sensors for reverse osmosis (RO) and forward osmosis (FO) desalination must separate reversible concentration polarization (CP) from irreversible mineral scaling and biofouling while remaining resilient to sensor drift, temperature shocks, and reference-channel contamination. We identify two structural vulnerabilities in differential membrane diagnostics: (1) a 2-arm differential cartridge cannot distinguish reference-arm contamination from test-arm cleanliness, producing a 71.17% estimation error without warning under 10% partial reference fouling (Scenario NC5), whereas a 3-arm differential manifold with a witness-ratio guard (τref = |rref(t) − rref,0|/rref,0 > 0.03) restores Rank-2 Fisher observability (det I > 0) and cuts error to 7.72%; and (2) autonomous diagnostic codebases suffer from oracle leakage when simulator ground-truth fields (ground_truth_scale_um) or synthetic nominal reference values remain accessible inside production classes or when invariants rely on strip-prone assert statements under python -O. After hardening CommercialPhysicalWitnessB (removing all simulator fields, enforcing explicit runtime ValueError guards across 19/19 standard and -O unit tests), the zero-oracle estimator achieves 5/5 (100%) clean operating-sweep coverage and reduces false-confident commits on 9 adversarial fault challenges from 7/9 (77.8%, SystemA) and 8/9 (88.9%, SystemC/R0) to 1/9 (11.1%, residual C07 80 nm sub-resolution CaSO4 film), while correctly abstaining (21/21 ABSTAIN_MISSING_REFERENCE_EVIDENCE) on 21 published literature rows that lack a physical reference channel.

Evidence classification: simulation only (SIMULATION_VERIFIED_WET_LAB_UNTESTED). No wet-lab membrane experiment has been executed; zero wet-lab membrane hours. Published as a methods protocol / registered-protocol preprint, not as experimental results. The \$551.32 COTS benchtop flow-loop protocol in Section 3 is pre-registered and specified, not run. All metrics are simulation replays and literature-row audits, deterministically reproduced by reproduce_paper2_zero_oracle_pareto.py, included in the reproducibility bundle. Reproducibility code in the bundle is Apache License 2.0; paper text is CC BY 4.0.

custody_records.raw_content: This paper systematizes typical feedwater quality requirements for AWE systems and explains why the parameters of specific electrical resistance (resistivity) and electrical conductivity are interrelated quality-control indicators. The main technological solutions for producing demineralized water are reviewed, including mechanical filtration, activated carbon filtration, reverse osmosis (RO), and electrodeionization (EDI). Key operational risks are also discussed, such as channeling, increased pressure drop (ΔP), carryover of carbon fines, biofouling, and oxidative damage to RO membranes. As a practical example, an aggregated process scheme is presented for a water treatment line designed to produce demineralized (DM) water with a target quality of approximately 1 MΩ·cm or higher. Recommendations are provided for monitoring (conductivity/resistivity, SiO₂, TOC, Cl⁻, iron), filter backwash regimes, protection of RO membranes from chlorine, and reduction of factors that contribute to increased cell voltage during AWE operation.

custody_records.raw_content: Reverse osmosis (RO) is the most common method for treating salt and brackish water. As a membrane-driven process, a key challenge for RO systems is their susceptibility to scaling and biofouling. To address these issues, functional coatings utilizing metal nanoparticles (MNPs) are developed. In this study, silver, gold, and copper nanoparticles are applied onto thin-film composite (TFC) membranes using plasma-enhanced magnetron sputtering. The elemental composition, surface morphology, and hydrophilicity of the coatings are analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and contact angle measurements. The antimicrobial properties and the filtration efficiency of the coated membranes are assessed through application-specific experimental setups. Silver and copper nanoparticles exhibit superior antimicrobial properties, reducing microorganism adhesion by a factor of 103 compared to uncoated membranes. Under appropriate coating conditions, no deterioration in filtration performance is observed. Enhancing the adhesion of MNPs is necessary for achieving sustained release of metal ions.

custody_records.raw_content: Graphyne-4 sheet exhibits promising potential for nanoscale desalination to achieve both high water permeability and salt rejection rate. Extensive molecular dynamics simulations on pore-size effects suggest that graphyne-4, with 4 acetylene bonds between two adjacent phenyl rings, has the best performance with 100% salt rejection and an unprecedented water permeability, to our knowledge, of ~13L/cm2/day/MPa, about 10 times higher than the state-of-the-art nanoporous graphene reported previously (Nano Lett.s 2012, 12, 3602-3608). In addition, the membrane entails very low energy consumption for producing 1m3 of fresh water, i.e., 3.6e-3 kWh/m3, three orders of magnitude less than the prevailing commercial membranes based on reverse osmosis. Water flow rate across the graphyne-4 sheet exhibits intriguing nonlinear dependence on the pore size owing to the quantized nature of water flow at the nanoscale. Such novel transport behavior has important implications to the design of highly effective and efficient desalination membranes.

custody_records.raw_content: Nanoporous carbon composite membranes, comprising a layer of porous carbon fiber structures with an average channel width of 30-60 nm grown on a porous ceramic substrate, are found to exhibit robust desalination effect with high freshwater flux. In three different membrane processes of vacuum membrane distillation, reverse osmosis and forward osmosis, the carbon composite membrane showed 100% salt rejection with 3.5 to 20 times higher freshwater flux compared to existing polymeric membranes. Thermal accounting experiments found that at least 80% of the freshwater pass through the carbon composite membrane with no phase change. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a unique salt rejection mechanism. When seawater is interfaced with either vapor or the surface of carbon, one to three interfacial atomic layers contain no salt ions. Below the liquid entry pressure, the salt solution is stopped at the openings to the porous channels and forms a meniscus, while the surface layer of freshwater can feed the surface diffusion flux that is fast-transported on the surfaces of the carbon fibers, driven by the chemical potential gradient. As the surface-transported water does not involve a phase change, hence that component involves no energy expenditure in the form of latent heat.

custody_records.raw_content: The reverse osmosis membrane module is an integral element of a desalination system as it determines the overall performance of the desalination plant. The fraction of clean water that can be recovered via this process is often limited by salt precipitation which plays a critical role in its sustainability. In this work, we present a model to study the complex interplay between flow, transport and precipitation processes in reverse osmosis membranes, which together influence recovery and in turn process sustainability. A reactive porous interface model describes the membrane with a dynamic evolving porosity and permeability to capture the scaling and clogging of the membrane. An open-source finite-volume numerical solver is implemented within the OpenFOAM library and numerical tests are presented here showing the effect of the various parameters of the model and the robustness of the model to describe a wide range of operating conditions.

custody_records.raw_content: Electrochemical desalination devices that use redox-active cation intercalation electrodes show promise for desalination of salt-rich water resources with high water recovery and low energy consumption. While previous modeling and experiments used ion-exchange membranes to maximize charge efficiency, here a membrane-free alternative is evaluated to reduce capital cost by using a porous diaphragm to separate Na$_{1+x}$NiFe(CN)$_6$ electrodes. Two-dimensional porous-electrode modeling shows that, while charge efficiency losses are inherent to a diaphragm-based architecture, charge efficiency values approaching the anion transference number (61$\%$ for NaCl) are achievable for diaphragms with sufficiently low salt conductance. Closed-form equations are thereby derived that relate charge efficiency to the non-dimensional Pèclet and Damköhler numbers that enable the selection of current and flow velocity to produce a desired degree of desalination. Simulations using these conditions are used to quantify the tradeoffs between energy consumption and salt removal rate for diaphragm-based cells operated at a range of currents. The simulated distributions of reactions are shown to result from the local salt concentration variations within electrodes using diffusion-potential theory. We also simulate the cycling dynamics of various flow configurations and show that flow-through electrodes exceed the degree-of-desalination compared with flow-by and flow-behind configurations due to solution stagnation within electrodes.

custody_records.raw_content: Three epochs in development of chemical dynamics are presented. We try to understand the modern research programs in the light of classical works. Three eras (or waves) of chemical dynamics can be revealed in the flux of research and publications. These waves may be associated with leaders: the first is the van't Hoof wave, the second may be called the Semenov--Hinshelwood wave and the third is definitely the Aris wave. Of course, the whole building was impossible without efforts of hundreds of other researchers. Some of of them are mentioned in our brief review.

custody_records.raw_content: Inverter-based resources (IBR) have been widely studied for their advantages on the current power systems. This increase in the penetration of renewable energy has raised some concerns about the stability of the existing grid. Historically, power systems are dominated by synchronous generators that can easily react to system instability due to high inertia and damping characteristics. However, with IBR, the control of the inverter plays a crucial role in contributing to the system stability and enhancing the functionality of the inverters. One of these novel control methods is droop control. Droop characteristics are used to control voltage, frequency, and active and reactive power. This paper presents the impact of frequency droop damping on system frequency, real power, and the rate of change of frequency with distributed energy resources. Also, battery sizing is suggested based on the results. The results also show the need for optimal selection for the frequency droop damping to fulfill the appropriate battery size in terms of cost and performance. The simulations are carried out in an electromagnetic transient program (EMTP)
